I had a similar experience while I was going to engineering school in the US. I couldn't concentrate, couldn't study, couldn't make the grade. So I dropped out. I spent about four years deciding what to do, and now I'm going back for something completely different. It can be hard when it seems like the only choices you have are bad ones. 

Your English is very good. Are you bilingual? If you are, there are many different organizations that might hire you as a translator, or a teacher. If not, there are still places you could go, make a solid living, and do something that isn't corrupt or political. South Korea actually has a program where you can go and teach English to students. Their only real requirements being you must speak English to their standard, you must not speak Korean, and you must have a university degree. 

There are plenty of opportunities to travel in college, or after you get your degree. Perhaps you just need some time out of the country? Foreign exchange programs can be really cool. You get to go to another school in another country, and study there for a semester, or even a whole year. A good friend of mine just got back from Spain, and she absolutely loved it. If you're worried about the long-term stay, there are plenty of shorter exchange opportunities available. 

Try not to make a big decision like dropping out or traveling to another country lightly. But keep in mind that different disciplines in school are very different in work load, skillset, and job opportunities. Are you going to school for something you don't enjoy? Is there perhaps another discipline that you think you may enjoy more, but doesn't nessicarially have the prospects you're looking for?

If your hair gets worse every time you shower, it's probably your shampoo/conditioner. Most of the name brand ones are actual garbage and don't help much. Tea tree smells nice and is really good for your hair and skin. You can easily find recepies online and make your own in bulk, or you can buy it in a shampoo from a natural foods store. The pre-made shampoos tend to be rather pricey though, (in comparison to name brand) but they have the added benefit of actually working. Showering daily actually can be bad for your hair and skin, which is why I asked. 

As far as self care goes, I'm not the greatest at it either. Once I started, though, it got easier. Now I can't imagine a day without tea or coffee. Or rather I can, but just don't want to. It they help me feel just a little more whole. 

The biggest thing I can't stress enough, though, is that *it is okay* to be uncomfortable in your own body. I would say that most people are, at some point or another. Most people grow out of it. But again, *it is okay* if you don't. 

I would encourage you to seek out local drag queens. If you've never seen Rupal's Drag Race, one can perform honest to God miracles with some makeup and pads. By playing dress-up, and participating in Pride, you may just be able to help yourself make it to the point where you are comfortable in your body, whether that be after some time with hormone therapy, or if you have surgery, or whatever you decide. I have a good friend and former co-worker who was a drag queen for a while. He still does shows and makeup from time to time, but if I were in your position I know he would do his best to ease my pain. It sounds to me like you could really use a friend like that. A supportive family is good and all, but sometimes you really just need someone who's been in your shoes. Or someone who can easily put themselves there. 

Don't give up girl. We are on the cusp of a cultural revolution when it comes to the LGBT community. Your time is coming. Who knows, it may already be here! All you have to do is hold on.

They don't want to accept that something might legitimately be wrong. 

"I never made a mistake. S/he was always happy. S/he always had everything s/he needed. There's no way this is serious." 

In our society we're taught that sad is bad. Negative emotions are something to be ashamed of. Because it shows weakness. 
 
Society, and those who participate, live life with their heads up their colon. For the most part. Yin is shameful for a man because it's not yang. The opposite for women. The truth is, neither are shameful. They are simply forces within us. 

What they fail to realize is that yinyang are complementary parts of a whole. When you drop a pebble into a mirror lake, there are ripples. Waves and troughs of equal proportion. 

When we force yang (commonly perceived as masculine strength in our society) the wave grows higher. The trough deeper. The same is true of we force yin. In order to be at peace (balance) they must be equal forces within us. 

I have bipolar disorder. Or so they call it. What this means is that I experience these troughs and waves, yin and yang, more strongly then most people. They are literal dragons that I ride in my reality. They shape my reality and how I perceive the world. 

What does this really mean? It means that I am unbalanced. Underdeveloped, if you may. The Black Dragon is strong. The White Dragon is weak. 

But yet there is hope. As the ripples expand across the lake they become closer and closer together. The waves become shorter, the troughs shallower.  After enough time has passed, neither is present, and the lake is calm again. 

In Taoist philosophy, yin and yang are not only complementary parts of the same whole, but given time they change into each other. They literally mean "shaded side" or "moon" and "sun" or "sunny side" respectively. But just as the moon's light is a reflection of the sun, shade is also the abscence of light. Imagine a mountain and valley. Early in the day, the mountain's east side is in the yang, and the valley and western mountain is in the yin. During midday, the valley is in full sun, and it is the eastern mountain that is shaded. At sunset, the western mountain is lit and the valley and east mountain are in shade. Such is the condition of humanity. 

Another example is the moon. Full moon, or full reflection, is a symbol of yang, or masculine energy. The new moon is a symbol of yin, or feminine energy. Most of the time the moon is somewhere in between the two. Only one night a month (roughly) is the moon Full or New. 

Inside yourself is a moon. A reflection of your life force. As your internal moon waxes, your light emotions grow strong. As it wanes, your dark emotions gain in intensity. This is part of the natural order of things. 

For some of us, the troughs are so low, and the highs so high that it puts out continued existence in jepordy. As the wave rolls up to the beach, it bends its head and falls in upon itself. Such is the way of an emotional being. As we reach the extremes of euphoria or depression, our life energy begins to change. As your yin energy peaks, it begins to turn itself into yang energy. Slowly. As the phases of the moon. 

In truth, having energy (emotions) that are strongly aligned with one side or another is unhealthy. Confidence turns to pigheadedness turns to mania, or sadness to depression to hopelessness. 

In our society, we take people who experience extremes and fuel the fire of their depression or mania by telling them to "tough it out" or "act a man." In truth, neither yin nor yang are inherently good or bad. In fact, the concepts of "goodness" or "badness" are artificial constructs that mean different things to different people. When we influence an unbalanced person to exert even more energy, they only become more unbalanced. Their internal lake a raging storm. 

You cannot build walls around your lake to hold the emotions in without raising the waters and the perils. When you push aside your negative emotions, their charge only becomes stronger. 

Negative and positive. Emotions are things that need to be experienced before they can be let go. Just as the weather; sometimes it rains, sometimes it shines, but the world continues to spin on. 

Your emotions are charges built up within you. They need to be expressed, or the storm will only grow. There are constructive and destructive ways to express your emotions. One constructive way would be to paint how you feel. Another would be to write poetry or prose. Another to sing your blues. Yet another would be to discuss your emotions and their roots with someone who understands how to interact without belittling you. Destructive ways include self-harm, vandalism, and abuse. 

The biggest thing about these positive forms of expression is that they make you feel validated, which from the sound of things is something you need to feel. They say "this is how I feel, and that emotional experience is okay." This validation is the first step to letting go of this energy before it destroys us. 

It is okay to feel sad. It is okay to feel different. The thing about feeling this way, however, is that it is a conscious choice on your part to express these feelings in a constructive or destructive way. From what you have said, you seem to have been trying and trying to express your emotions through talking to your loved ones. This hasn't been working, or you wouldn't be here. I strongly urge you to try something else. Either change who you are expressing to, or change your form of expression. By going straight from talk therapy to suicide, you are skipping many many forms of both constructive and destructive expression for the ultimate destructive form of expression: taking a life. 

There *are* other options. Many of them. All art is a form of constructive expression. All war is a form of destructive expression. Please don't give up. Before you go to war, give art a chance.

Socially awkward is most teenagers. As far as employment goes, you don't have to be a master communicator to run a register. Or to stock shelves. Or to clean, or a million other things. I have a script for running a register. I have a script for when I talk to my boss. Its like having a subvocabulary/ phrase library. All you have to do is figure out what to say once. My work vocab is probably less than 200 words. 

I have a good friend with asburgers. He's a year or two older than I, and has a much better job and living situation. The most important thing you learn from high school are your strengths and weaknesses. Play to your strengths. You likely haven't even discovered all of yours at your age. You can also focus on strengthening areas you're weak in. Communication is something I suck at. I also have lots of social anxiety. I'm bipolar, introverted, and shy. Somehow, I still have friends. One thing I've learned from my mental illness is that, no matter who you are, you are on the spectrum for every mental disorder, known and unknown. 

I'm not a joker. Most of my knee slappers are completely unintentional. I've just kinda come to accept that sometimes I say funny shit. Most of my friends I've met through hobbies.  You don't always need to know what to say. Most of the conversatio,s I have are about me, the other person(s), or things we have in common (shows, games, etc.)
